nameStory: The 'showy' in showy mountain-ash refers to this tree's spectacular clusters of bright white flowers in spring and brilliant orange-red berries in fall that really steal the show. Despite its name, it's not a true ash tree at all – it's actually in the rose family! The 'mountain-ash' name comes from its compound leaves that look similar to true ash trees, plus its preference for cooler, higher elevation spots.
description: Showy mountain-ash is a small deciduous tree or large shrub that typically grows 15-25 feet tall in New England. It has a rounded crown and compound leaves made up of many leaflets arranged along a central stem, giving it a delicate, feathery appearance. In late spring, it produces showy flat-topped clusters of small white flowers that later develop into bright orange-red berry clusters that persist well into fall. This hardy northern species is perfectly adapted to New England's cooler climates.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Compound leaves with 11-15 narrow, toothed leaflets arranged along a reddish central stem. Each leaflet is 2-4 inches long with sharp teeth along the edges and feels smooth to the touch with prominent veins underneath.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Dense, flat-topped clusters of small white flowers in late spring, each flower about 1/3 inch across with 5 petals. The clusters can be 3-5 inches wide and have a sweet, somewhat medicinal smell.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Bright orange-red berries in large drooping clusters that ripen in late summer and fall. Each berry is about 1/3 inch across, feels firm when fresh, and contains small seeds. Birds love them!

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Smooth gray bark on young trees becoming slightly scaly with age. The bark feels relatively smooth compared to most trees and may have lighter horizontal lines called lenticels.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Small tree or large shrub with an oval to rounded crown. Branches tend to be somewhat ascending, and the overall shape is neat and symmetrical when grown in the open.

habitat: Showy mountain-ash thrives in cooler spots throughout New England, especially at higher elevations in the mountains and along rocky shores near large lakes. You'll often find it growing in acidic, well-drained soils in clearings, forest edges, and rocky slopes where it gets plenty of sunlight. It's particularly common in the White Mountains, Green Mountains, and along the Maine coast where cool, moist conditions suit it perfectly.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge with a reddish tint in late April to May, followed by spectacular flat-topped clusters of white flowers in late May to early June that attract many pollinators.
seasonality.summer: Fully leafed with bright green compound foliage. Green berry clusters begin developing and gradually start changing color by late summer.
seasonality.fall: Brilliant orange-red berry clusters reach peak color in September and October, while leaves turn yellow to orange before dropping. Berries often persist after leaves fall.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches reveal smooth gray bark and plump reddish-brown buds. Some berry clusters may still cling to branches, providing winter food for birds.

funFact: Despite producing thousands of bright berries that look deliciously edible, showy mountain-ash berries are quite bitter and astringent when raw – but many Indigenous peoples traditionally cooked them into jellies and sauces, and they're still used today to make mountain-ash jelly that tastes somewhat like cranberries!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with American mountain-ash, but showy mountain-ash has wider leaflets that are broader at the base and larger, showier flower and fruit clusters. Remember: 'showy' means bigger and bolder clusters! European mountain-ash (rowan) has similar berries but more leaflets per leaf (usually 13-17 vs 11-15).
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the name fool you – mountain-ash trees are not related to true ash trees (like white ash or green ash) at all! They're actually members of the rose family, closely related to apples and hawthorns. The name confusion dates back centuries when European settlers noticed the similar compound leaves and just assumed they were related.
compareHints: Showy mountain-ash stands out from its cousins with its broader leaflets and more robust flower and fruit clusters – everything about it is just a bit bigger and showier than American mountain-ash. Compared to the common European mountain-ash (rowan), showy mountain-ash typically has fewer, broader leaflets and is better adapted to New England's harsh winters. The berry clusters also tend to be larger and more prominent in the showy species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: American mountain ash differs from European mountain ash (the more common rowan) by having more leaflets per leaf (13-17 vs 9-15) and slightly smaller berry clusters.

European mountain ash can be distinguished from its native cousin, American mountain ash, by its leaflets - European has 9-15 leaflets per leaf while American typically has 11-17, and European's leaflets are less hairy underneath.
